description: Designing a physical 2-axis servo gimbal prototype that translates real NASA lunar South Pole latitude, longitude, and elevation datasets into physical actuation angles. Built to demonstrate automated lander sensor pointing and terrain tracking for Artemis-era missions.
summary:
The Lunar South Pole 2-Axis Actuation Gimbal is a physical hardware prototype built for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. While many navigation tools focus purely on software maps, real lunar landers and surface assets rely on precise mechanical actuation to orient sensors, high-gain communication antennas, and solar arrays in the Moon's extreme south polar terrain.
This prototype bridges real NASA lunar coordinate datasets—including latitude, longitude, and altitude/elevation angles—directly with physical motion. A Python serial pipeline reads live coordinate data and translates spatial parameters into real-time Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) commands for a dual-servo 2-axis gimbal. By physically demonstrating how trajectory and terrain elevation angles drive mechanical pointing in real time, this project offers a low-cost, tangible testbed for validating autonomous sensor alignment and terrain-tracking hardware for Artemis-era lunar south pole missions.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

The Lunar South Pole 2-Axis Actuation Gimbal is a physical hardware-in-the-loop prototype built for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. It demonstrates how a lunar lander or surface communication terminal at the Moon's South Pole (0°E, -90°N) physically tracks Earth for continuous Direct-to-Earth (DTE) telemetry and navigation support.

  • Data Generation: Using the NASA JPL Horizons System, we generated an observer ephemeris table from the Lunar South Pole (0°E, -90°N, 0 km elevation) targeting Earth across a multi-week mission window (2026-11-14 to 2026-12-14).
  • Serial Data Streaming: A Python script parses the real NASA azimuth, elevation, and spatial coordinate angles from the dataset, normalizes the angular values, and streams them live via USB serial communication to a microcontroller.
  • 2-Axis Mechanical Actuation: The microcontroller translates incoming serial data into precise Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) signals, driving two orthogonally mounted servo motors (azimuth pan and elevation tilt) to physically point the payload toward Earth's shifting position in the lunar south polar sky.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Bridging Data to Hardware: While many navigation solutions stop at software visualization, real Artemis-era lunar surface operations depend on reliable mechanical pointing for high-gain antennas, optical communications, and solar arrays.
  • Low-Cost Mission Testbed: This prototype provides an accessible, real-time physical verification rig for testing antenna pointing algorithms and mechanical tracking limits before deploying expensive flight hardware.

Tools, Languages & Hardware Used

  • NASA Data: NASA JPL Horizons Web Application (Solar System Dynamics Observer Table).
  • Software & Languages: Python (data parsing and PySerial telemetry streaming) and C++/Arduino firmware (PWM servo control).
  • Hardware: ESP32 microcontroller board, solderless breadboard, two micro-servo motors arranged in a 2-axis gimbal mount, and a host laptop for live serial monitoring.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered

  • Creativity: Instead of building a purely digital dashboard, we transformed abstract orbital ephemeris tables into tangible, real-time robotic motion that judges can visually verify.
  • Key Engineering Factors:
    • Lunar South Pole Geometry: At -90°N latitude, Earth hovers very low near the lunar horizon and oscillates due to lunar libration, making continuous elevation and azimuth tracking critical to avoid terrain obstruction from crater rims.
    • Servo Mapping & Range Limits: We accounted for mechanical deadbands, angular scaling, and smooth step transitions so the servos track coordinate updates accurately without jitter or over-rotation.
